title: CryoVault 2.0

candidates.docstring:
CRYOVAULT 2.0 -- seal tool.

Ships to players. Contains no answers: every key is derived from what you
supply on the command line.

    # you solved stage 1; open the stage 2 record with its answer
    python3 unseal.py 1 "<your stage 1 answer>"

    # once you hold all ten, open the vault
    python3 unseal.py vault "<a1>" "<a2>" ... "<a10>"

Each record is sealed with AES-256-GCM, so a wrong answer fails cleanly rather
than handing you plausible garbage. Answers are trimmed and lowercased before
use; nothing else about them is forgiving.

Opening a record takes a second or two and about 134 MB of memory. That is
deliberate: the sealed records are in your hands, so the seal is keyed through
a memory-hard derivation to make guessing answers expensive rather than free.

Requires: pip install cryptography
candidates.review_reason: Referenced by writeup; requires logic/dependency review

candidates.docstring:
FrostRNG sealing routine -- RECOVERED / RECONSTRUCTED FROM MEMORY.

    STATUS: reconstruction. The original seal.py was on the node when it
    sealed. This file was rewritten from memory by ops during the 2.0
    handover and has NOT been executed since. It is believed correct and
    was verified against the manifest at the time, but it may contain
    transcription errors -- the constants in particular were copied by
    hand off a whiteboard photograph.

    If it does not reproduce the self-test vector in the sealed manifest
    header, trust the vector, not this file. The constants were transcribed
    digit by digit and a SINGLE DIGIT is the most likely thing to be wrong --
    the vector is short, so checking candidates against it is cheap.

FrostRNG is a 64-bit LCG. Only the top eight bits of each state are emitted,
so the keystream discards 56 bits per byte. Ops considered this adequate.

The seal is keyed on the exact second of sealing. Only the date was written
down. This was raised at the time.

candidates.docstring:
Batched version of the public thaw-ladder solve.

The public solver's byte search is sequential (one round trip per candidate).
This version sends all 256 candidates for a ladder rung in one batch.  Every
wrong candidate has the same cost, so the first meter deviation in the batch is
the matching byte.  That cuts wall time enough to fit inside the service's
connection lifetime.

candidates.docstring:
Exploit thawd 7.3's signed SEAL offset and coarsened work meter.

SEAL accepts negative 16-bit offsets, so offset 0x8000 compares a location in
ordinary RAM with the secret profile.  The field meter is floor(work/q): each
matching profile byte contributes one unit.  We align every wrong guess to
residue q-1, turning the next matching byte into a visible +1 meter tick.

title: MURMUR v1.2 Mesh Control Protocol

candidates.docstring:
MURMUR v1.2 / broken_telephone exploit.

Vulnerabilities
---------------
1. The node reuses one ChaCha20-Poly1305 one-time key for every n2g transport
   message: the ChaCha20 keystream is frozen across all frames, so a chosen
   plaintext can be encrypted without knowing any key, and the Poly1305 tag is
   computed from a frozen (r, s).
2. Because the tag *is* verified, the frozen Poly1305 key has to be recovered
   first.  Poly1305 is linear in the key: for two frames whose AEAD macdata
   share a block prefix and have the same block count,

       acc_B - acc_A = sum_i (nB_i - nA_i) * r**(N-i)  (mod 2**130-5)

   The tag difference cancels s, and since every ciphertext delta is directly
   observable this collapses to a quadratic congruence in r, solved exactly.
3. The gateway's own responses share a single frozen keystream whose payload is
   zero padded, so XOR-ing the admin response ciphertext against a captured
   gateway response yields the provisioning secret in the clear.

Exploit: recover the frozen n2g keystream (from the telemetry DATA frame's known
fields plus the zero-payload CONTROL keepalives) and the frozen Poly1305 key,
forge `PROVISION / role=admin`, inject it, then decrypt the reply.

Usage: python3 exploit.py [host] [port]

candidates.docstring:
MURMUR tap client / recon+exploit toolkit.

Usage:
    python3 murmur_tap_client.py pwn.h7tex.com 41531

What it does automatically:
  1. Connects to the tap (newline-delimited JSON over TCP, per MURMUR-1.2.md sec 5).
  2. Logs every {"event":...} line it receives.
  3. Buffers raw wire bytes per direction (n2g = node->gateway, g2n = gateway->node).
  4. As soon as it has seen the 3 handshake messages, it recomputes `h2` the same
     way a passive observer can (h2 only depends on public transcript bytes: the
     gateway static pubkey, both ephemeral pubkeys, and the two handshake
     ciphertexts -- see MURMUR-1.2.md sec 1). No private key material is needed.
  5. Once h2 is known it can de-mask `masked_len` on every subsequent frame
     (mask_i = LE16(BLAKE2s(h2 || "MURMUR-len" || LE32(i)))), so it can find
     frame boundaries/types/lengths even though it can't decrypt the AEAD body
     (that still needs the real Noise transport key).
  6. Drops you into an interactive REPL so you can inspect frames and send
     `inject` / `step` / `close` commands per the tap protocol.

This is a recon + framework script -- it gets you transcript visibility and
frame boundaries "for free" as a passive tap. Actually forging an accepted
admin PROVISION command still requires finding the real protocol bug (nonce
reuse, replay, KCI, etc.) which is easiest to spot once you can see live
frame metadata. Use `frames` in the REPL to inspect what's flowing after the
handshake completes.

candidates.docstring:
one-more  --  a blind Schnorr signing service (secp256k1).

Talk to it one command per message:

    open                  -> "id <k> R <hex64>"      opens a signing session
    sign <k> <c>          -> "s <int>"               one challenge per session
    submit                -> then send ONE more message, a JSON line:
                             [[msg_hex, Rx, Ry, s], ...]
    quit

On connect the service sends "X <hex64>" -- its public key for THIS connection.
Every connection is an independent instance with its own fresh key.

A signature (R, s) on m is valid iff   s*G == R + H(R,m)*X,
with H(R,m) = SHA256(x||y||m) mod n.

The service is blind: it never sees the message, only the scalar challenge you
hand it, and it answers each session exactly once. So it signs once per
session, and you walk away with one signature per session. That is the deal.

Hand back MORE valid signatures, on distinct messages, than the number of
challenges I answered, and you get the flag.

    python3 server.py                  # WebSocket on ws://127.0.0.1:1337
    python3 server.py --stdio          # one command per line on stdin

candidates.docstring:
KumoSec ChainVault - automated CTF solver (stdlib only, no pip deps).

Vulnerability chain
-------------------
1. The deployer/registry owner is the *ganache-cli default account #0*, so its
   well-known private key is public knowledge -> we can call the owner-only
   `AuditorRegistry.registerAuditor(ourWallet)`.
   (Fallback: brute-force a guessable `legacyMigrationTokens` seed and call the
   unauthenticated `migrateLegacyAuditor(addr, token)`.)
2. `ChainVault` has no owner withdrawal path. The only payout is
   `settleClaim()`, which pays `pendingClaims[msg.sender]`, and that mapping is
   zeroed *after* the ETH transfer (CEI violation -> classic reentrancy).
3. `pendingClaims` is capped at 1 ETH per finding, but nothing stops us from
   submitting a finding + settling once per bounty (6 x 1 ETH = 6 ETH).
4. When `address(this).balance <= emergencyThreshold` (threshold == 0),
   `_checkEmergencyCondition()` flips `emergencyMode`/`isSolved` to true, which
   is what `/api/v1/vault/flag` verifies.

Usage
-----
  python3 chainvault_solver.py <TEAM_TOKEN>
  python3 chainvault_solver.py <TEAM_TOKEN> --base http://host --out flag.txt
  python3 chainvault_solver.py --tokens tokens.txt        # batch, one per line

candidates.docstring:
Solve: Weighty Secrets (hardened, high-density Merkle-Hellman knapsack)

Setup recap
------------
- public_instance.json contains:
    n               : knapsack dimension (96)
    public_weights  : a_1..a_n  (the MH public key)
    ciphertext_sum  : c = sum(x_i * a_i), x_i in {0,1}   (x is a 96-bit secret)
    aes_nonce / aes_ciphertext : AES-256-GCM encryption of the flag,
                                 key = SHA256(secret_bytes), secret packed MSB-first/byte

Attack
------
The public weights were generated as a_i = r*b_i mod q for a tight
superincreasing sequence b (density ~0.90-0.92, just under the CJLOS
theoretical bound of 0.9408). Because density is this high, a *plain*
LLL pass on the naive subset-sum lattice will almost never find the
target vector directly -- you need the CJLOS "balanced" lattice
construction below AND a proper BKZ reduction (not just LLL) with a
non-trivial block size (try block_size=20, then increase toward
30-40 if it doesn't pop out). This is the part that costs real time:
expect several BKZ tours at dimension 97, which is genuinely a
30-90 minute exercise on a laptop even with fpylll, not a
copy-paste-and-done LLL script.

Lattice (dimension n+1 = 97), CJLOS balanced construction:
  row_i (i=1..n): 2*e_i  followed by  N*a_i
  row_{n+1}     : (1,1,...,1) followed by N*c
A shortest vector of the form (+-1,...,+-1, 0) reveals x_i = (1+s_i)/2.
N should be on the order of sqrt(n) to a small multiple of it -- tune
if the first attempt doesn't surface a 0/±1 vector.
